paragraphs.title: Human Life as Hard Labor and Prolonged Suffering

answers: Like the days of a servant and a hireling
easy.explanation: Job compares human life to the days of a servant and a hireling.
easy.q: How does Job describe man's days upon earth?

easy.explanation: Job says that a hireling looks for “the reward of his work.”
easy.q: What does a hireling look for?

answers: Wearisome nights and tossing to and fro
easy.explanation: Job describes wearisome nights and tossing until the dawning of the day.
easy.q: What does Job experience during the night?

answers: A life marked by labor and hardship
A life of success and wealth
medium.explanation: Both comparisons present life as difficult labor and suffering.
medium.q: What do the images of a servant and a hireling communicate about Job's life?

answers: Months that seem empty and without profit
medium.explanation: Job regards his months as vain, empty, and without meaningful relief.
medium.q: What does Job mean by “months of vanity”?

medium.explanation: His pain and misery keep him restless while he waits for morning.
medium.q: What causes Job to toss to and fro through the night?

answers: From labor and suffering to bodily decay and loss of hope
challenge.explanation: Job moves from images of hard labor to sickness, decay, and days spent without hope.

answers: That life is long and stable
That a person is preparing for work
challenge.explanation: Job says his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, stressing their rapid passing.
challenge.q: What does the image of the weaver's shuttle emphasize?

answers: His body grows stronger as time passes
Time stops because of his sickness
His days pass quickly while his body breaks down
challenge.explanation: Job joins the brevity of his days with the decay of his flesh and skin.
challenge.q: How do the descriptions of Job's body and time form one picture?

paragraphs.title: The Transience of Life and the Irreversibility of Death

easy.q: To what does Job compare his life?

easy.explanation: Job says, “mine eye shall no more see good.”
easy.q: What does Job say his eye shall no more see?

answers: He begins a new earthly life
He does not come up again
easy.explanation: Job says that the one who goes down to the grave “shall come up no more.”
easy.q: What happens to the person who goes down to the grave?

answers: Both emphasize passing away and disappearance
medium.explanation: As a cloud is consumed and vanishes, so human life passes away.
medium.q: What connection does Job make between a cloud and human life?

answers: The person will no longer hear Job's voice
The person will no longer see Job
The person will forget Job's name
medium.explanation: The statement refers to Job's disappearance from the sight of the living.
medium.q: In Job 7:8, what does “shall see me no more” mean?

answers: He has gone on a short journey
medium.explanation: Job presents death as a departure from which a person does not return.
medium.q: What follows from Job's statement that a dead man does not return to his house?

answers: The desire to see good again versus the brevity of life
challenge.explanation: Job longs for good, yet he emphasizes that life quickly passes and death ends earthly return.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in Job 7:7–10?

answers: Wind is associated with a house
challenge.explanation: The comparison shows how quickly Job's life is passing away.
challenge.q: Why does the image of wind strengthen Job's sense of urgency?

answers: From the house toward renewed life
From wind and cloud to no return to the house
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from fleeting life to disappearance in death and permanent separation from home.
challenge.q: How does the imagery of disappearance develop through these verses?

paragraphs.title: Protest Against Suffering and the Plea for Rest

easy.explanation: Job says, “I will not refrain my mouth,” but will speak in anguish and bitterness.
easy.q: How does Job decide to respond to his suffering?

easy.explanation: Although he expects his bed to comfort him, dreams and visions terrify him instead.
Job says that his soul chooses death rather than his life.
easy.q: What does Job prefer because of his suffering?

answers: He is in anguish of spirit and bitterness of soul
medium.explanation: Job explains that his speech comes from anguish and bitterness.
medium.q: Why does Job speak instead of remaining silent?

answers: He feels treated as a target for divine attention and affliction
He is asking for a place of rest
medium.explanation: Job asks why he has been set as a mark, or target, against God.
medium.q: What does Job mean by asking whether he is “a mark” watched by God?

answers: They remind him of his home
medium.explanation: Job says that God scares him with dreams and terrifies him through visions.
medium.q: How do dreams increase Job's suffering?

answers: To suggest that he is a dangerous power requiring watchfulness
To show that he wants to rule the sea
To compare himself to a servant
challenge.explanation: Job questions why God watches him as though he were a dangerous creature.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of Job's question, “Am I a sea, or a whale”?

answers: Sleep becomes a source of comfort
Sleep, which should comfort him, becomes a source of fear
challenge.explanation: His bed and couch promise relief, but dreams and visions make the night terrifying.
challenge.q: What change occurs in Job's view of sleep?

answers: Job views his suffering as light and temporary
Job has found a practical solution to his troubles
His suffering is so severe that he desires complete release
challenge.explanation: When even sleep offers no relief, Job says that his soul chooses death rather than life.
challenge.q: What does the movement from sleep to death reveal?

paragraphs.title: Questioning Divine Attention and Asking for Forgiveness

answers: Why God magnifies man and sets His heart upon him
easy.explanation: Job asks, “What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him?”
easy.q: What does Job question about man's position before God?

easy.explanation: Job says that God visits him every morning and tries him every moment.
easy.q: How often does Job say that God visits and tries man?

easy.explanation: Job asks God to pardon his transgression, take away his iniquity, and leave him alone.
easy.q: What does Job ask for at the end of his speech?

answers: As a way to forget his pain
medium.explanation: Job experiences God's visitation and testing as relentless scrutiny rather than comfort.
medium.q: How does Job experience God's close attention?

answers: He asks God never to forgive him
He asks God to stop pursuing and afflicting him
He says God cannot see him
medium.explanation: Job asks why God will not leave him alone and give him relief.
medium.q: What does Job mean when he asks, “How long wilt thou not depart from me”?

answers: He is preparing to leave his house
He wants to receive a reward
He feels that death is near and time is running out
medium.explanation: Job says that he will soon sleep in the dust, so he asks for forgiveness before death.

answers: He recognizes God's attention but asks God to leave him alone
He claims that God knows nothing about him
challenge.explanation: Job acknowledges that God watches and tests him, yet pleads for that attention to cease.
challenge.q: What tension appears in Job's words about God's attention?

answers: Both emphasize the severity of suffering and the nearness of death
challenge.explanation: The first expresses relentless distress, while the second points to Job's approaching death.
challenge.q: How are “till I swallow down my spittle” and “I shall sleep in the dust” related?

answers: That God ignore him without offering pardon
That God pardon his transgression and take away his iniquity
challenge.explanation: Job's confession leads to a plea for forgiveness and the removal of his guilt.
